Troubleshooting Linux Systems

1. Troubleshooting Linux Systems

Troubleshooting is controlled reduction of uncertainty. The goal is not to try the greatest number of commands. It is to identify the smallest useful next observation while preserving the ability to recover. HarborWorks adopts one investigation record so different administrators can continue the same incident without repeating risky experiments.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Chapter 23 — Troubleshooting Linux Systems

2. Choose the next discriminating test

Prefer the smallest test that distinguishes plausible causes; verify the original symptom after the smallest justified change. A reinstall changes unrelated state before the failed layer is identified.

SOURCE: Choose the next discriminating test

3. Chapter 23 — Troubleshooting Linux Systems

Troubleshooting is controlled reduction of uncertainty. The goal is not to try the greatest number of commands. It is to identify the smallest useful next observation while preserving the ability to recover. HarborWorks adopts one investigation record so different administrators can continue the same incident without repeating risky experiments.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Chapter 23 — Troubleshooting Linux Systems

4. 23.1 A Systematic Troubleshooting Method

State the symptom in observable terms: who is affected, what fails, when it began, and what still works. Draw the relevant path. Gather the existing state, propose competing explanations, select a discriminating test, and record its outcome. Make a bounded change only when the evidence and authority justify it.

Keep restoration and explanation distinct. Rolling back a release may restore service before the exact defect is known. That is often appropriate, but a successful rollback does not prove which line caused the failure. Preserve logs and artifacts so analysis can continue after users recover.

For each test, write the prediction before running it. “If the listener is absent, a local socket inspection will show no bound endpoint” is more useful than “try networking commands.” A test with no decision attached is often just activity.

Linux example — 23.1

Start with a time-stamped symptom snapshot.

What to check: Form a testable hypothesis before applying a repair.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.1 A Systematic Troubleshooting Method

What to check: Form a testable hypothesis before applying a repair.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.1 A Systematic Troubleshooting Method

6. 23.2 Establishing What Changed

Changes include deployments, package updates, certificate renewals, identity updates, data growth, network policy, external dependencies, and ordinary workload shifts. “Nobody changed the server” does not exclude any of those.

Compare configuration revisions, package transaction history, service start times, scheduled tasks, and the monitoring timeline. File modification times can help locate candidates but are not proof of author, intent, or causality. Clock offsets and deployment tools can also distort a superficial timeline.

Ask what changed in the failing path rather than collecting every change in the organization. Preserve the exact old and new artifacts when authorized. A diff supports a hypothesis, while reproduction or another discriminating observation strengthens the causal claim.

Linux example — 23.2

Inspect recent boots and configuration modification times.

What to check: Modification time is a clue, not proof of who changed a file or why.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.2 Establishing What Changed

8. 23.3 Service Failures

Inspect the service’s status, effective unit, journal, executable, configuration, and runtime identity. A service can fail before its application logger initializes, so the journal or supervisor may hold the only early evidence.

Use sudo only when needed to obtain the authorized view. A syntax error, missing binary, denied directory, occupied port, and start-rate limit call for different responses. Resetting a failure state or restarting does not fix the cause.

After repair, test the original client operation and persistence across a planned restart. A unit becoming active for one second is not enough to establish stable recovery.

Linux example — 23.3

Inspect the failed service and its bounded journal.

What to check: Use your affected unit; identify the first meaningful error rather than only the restart counter.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.3 Service Failures

11. 23.4 CPU Problems

Decide whether the problem is utilization, contention, throttling, or inefficient work. Check per-core activity, process and thread use, runnable tasks, cgroup limits, and application throughput. A legitimate batch job may use all allocated CPU without being unhealthy.

For a runaway process, preserve its identity, arguments where safe, service association, and recent logs. Use the application’s supported stop or supervisor first. Sending SIGKILL immediately removes some evidence and prevents ordinary cleanup.

If the host is still responsive, prefer a bounded observation interval before changing priorities or limits. Raising one task’s priority redistributes access; it does not create capacity. Test whether lower-priority services remain within their own requirements.

Linux example — 23.4

Rank process CPU usage and sample scheduling.

What to check: ps percentages and interval samples have different accounting windows.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.4 CPU Problems

13. 23.5 Memory Problems

Inspect host memory, process trends, service limits, kernel OOM records, and swap activity. A process disappearing with a memory-related event differs from an application refusing an allocation or a cgroup enforcing its maximum.

Choose the actual affected unit. Some properties depend on accounting and version support. Do not assume the named process is the cause merely because it was selected as a victim. Reconstruct demand and limits during the event.

A temporary restart can restore memory headroom while leaving a leak unresolved. Record how quickly pressure returns, preserve the release version, and schedule a reproducible investigation rather than normalizing periodic restarts as the only control.

Linux example — 23.5

Inspect availability and OOM evidence.

What to check: Connect a killed process with actual memory pressure or a configured limit.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.5 Memory Problems

16. 23.6 Disk-Full Conditions

Identify the filesystem that rejected the write, not merely the machine’s total free space. Inspect block capacity, inode capacity, quotas, mount state, and deleted-open files. A separate /var can be full while /home has ample space.

The GNU du example stays on one filesystem and limits displayed depth. It can still require significant I/O, and permission errors make its view incomplete. A discrepancy with df invites investigation, not blind deletion.

Prefer stopping the source of growth, preserving required evidence, and reclaiming known disposable data through its owner. Deleting database files, arbitrary logs, or package metadata can convert a capacity incident into data loss.

Linux example — 23.6

Compare filesystem capacity and visible allocation.

What to check: -x keeps the directory scan on one filesystem; large scans can still add I/O load.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.6 Disk-Full Conditions

19. 23.7 Inode Exhaustion

A filesystem can run out of file objects while retaining free data blocks. Many small files can consume inode capacity on filesystems with a bounded inode pool. df -i helps separate this from ordinary byte exhaustion; interpretation varies by filesystem design.

Find the responsible tree with bounded traversal. A broad recursive enumeration during an inode incident can add substantial load. Understand whether files are queue entries, session records, cache entries, or evidence before removing them.

Fix the retention or producer behavior as well as freeing space. Expanding or rebuilding storage without addressing unbounded file creation merely changes how long the same failure takes to recur.

Linux example — 23.7

Check inode capacity independently of bytes.

What to check: The bounded listing gives clues; avoid deleting files before identifying their owner and lifecycle.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.7 Inode Exhaustion

21. 23.8 Filesystem Problems

A filesystem can be mounted read-only after errors, missing, or backed by an unhealthy device. Inspect findmnt, the kernel journal, and the storage path. Distinguish a logical filesystem issue from repeated controller or medium errors.

Do not run a repair tool against a mounted writable filesystem unless its documentation explicitly supports the exact operation. ext4 and XFS have different tools and procedures. A tool’s “force” option is not a diagnostic strategy.

Protect valuable data before repair when possible, especially on unstable hardware. Record every repair action and retain its output. Repeatedly rerunning repairs on a failing device can reduce the chance of later recovery. (R21, R22)

Linux example — 23.8

Inspect mounts and kernel errors.

What to check: Do not run repair tools against a mounted filesystem to see what happens.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.8 Filesystem Problems

23. 23.9 Permission Problems

Trace the effective identity and complete path. Check parent traversal, owner/group modes, supplementary groups, ACL masks, mount options, SELinux or AppArmor, and service sandboxing. The login user’s access is not necessarily the application’s access.

Some tools need installation and SELinux output is meaningful only in the relevant environment. A successful sudo cat proves root can read the path; it does not test the service domain or sandbox.

The correct repair grants the intended operation at the layer that rejected it. Broad recursive permission changes destroy useful distinctions and can introduce write access to executable or secret material.

Linux example — 23.9

Trace credentials, path modes, and ACLs.

What to check: Substitute the failing path and also inspect SELinux or AppArmor evidence.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.9 Permission Problems

26. 23.10 DNS Problems

Compare the system’s name-service path with a direct DNS query. getent hosts NAME follows system configuration; dig NAME asks DNS through its configured or specified resolver. Different results can reveal hosts-file entries, search domains, caching, or resolver integration.

Record the exact name, query type, response status, server, and client network. An AAAA result with a broken IPv6 route can look like intermittent name trouble while the DNS answer is correct. A trailing dot denotes an absolute DNS name and can avoid search-domain expansion in a controlled test.

Do not replace managed resolver files with a public resolver as a universal repair. That can break internal names and disclose queries. Fix the managing service and intended resolver path. (R31)

Linux example — 23.10

Compare general resolution with DNS.

What to check: Disagreement can reveal NSS, local-hosts, or resolver-path differences.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.10 DNS Problems

28. 23.11 Network Problems

Work from local configuration toward the destination: interface state, address, route selection, neighbor resolution, host policy, upstream policy, remote listener, and application response. Check the return path too; asymmetric policy can allow a request out but block its reply.

Use a real approved destination instead of the example address. A route lookup reports a decision; it does not send an application request or prove remote reachability.

Do not bring down the management interface to “refresh” networking over the only SSH session. Establish console recovery before disruptive changes, and use the distribution’s manager for persistent configuration.

Linux example — 23.11

Inspect interfaces, routes, and socket state.

What to check: Test the specific destination only after the local observations explain the expected path.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.11 Network Problems

31. 23.12 SSH Failures

Separate connection establishment, server identity verification, user authentication, and session startup. A refused connection usually directs attention earlier in the path than “permission denied,” but intermediaries and policy can affect the exact symptom.

Use bounded client diagnostics such as ssh -v and correlate with server logs. Protect debug output because it can reveal usernames, hostnames, key paths, and authentication details. Verify host-key changes through an independent channel rather than deleting the known-host entry reflexively.

For authentication failures, inspect the selected key, account status, allowed methods, effective Match rules, file ownership, and central identity state. Keep the working session open while testing any correction from a new session. (R29)

Linux example — 23.12

Locate the SSH failure stage.

What to check: Requires the approved lab host; do not remove known_hosts entries merely to silence a changed-key warning.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.12 SSH Failures

33. 23.13 Package Problems

Identify whether the failure concerns repository reachability, trust, dependency resolution, locks, package scripts, or runtime behavior after installation. A package transaction failure and a successfully installed but incompatible application are different incidents.

Inspect package-manager history and the exact error. Do not disable signature verification or delete lock files simply to make the command proceed. An active transaction may be legitimately protecting its database.

Recovery can require repairing a partially configured package set through the distribution’s supported tools, then retesting services. On a healthy backed-up lab, dpkg --audit can reveal incomplete Debian-package state. Do not apply guessed repair commands to production without understanding the interrupted transaction and rollback limits.

Linux example — 23.13

Check package consistency using the applicable family.

What to check: Review transaction history and release compatibility before forcing reinstallations.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.13 Package Problems

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.13 Package Problems

35. 23.14 Kernel Problems

Kernel symptoms include device errors, hangs, panics, repeated driver faults, and resource-management events. Capture the running kernel, command line, relevant journal, hardware context, and recent package changes. A later reboot may erase volatile evidence if persistent logging or crash capture was not configured.

A known-good kernel can be a recovery option when its compatibility and security implications are reviewed. It is not proof that every problem after an update is a kernel regression. Firmware, external modules, storage, and changed application behavior can be involved.

Escalate with a reproducible case and exact versions. Avoid unloading a storage or network driver in a live service just because a module name appears near an error.

Linux example — 23.14

Read the running kernel and warning messages.

What to check: Installed kernel versions may differ from the one producing the current messages.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.14 Kernel Problems

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.14 Kernel Problems

37. 23.15 Boot Failures

Identify the last successful stage: firmware, bootloader, kernel, initramfs, root mount, systemd dependencies, or application startup. A blank web page after reboot does not establish a bootloader failure.

Use the console and known recovery media. In a rescue environment, determine which filesystem is mounted where before editing files; paths may refer to the rescue system rather than the installed system. Encryption and separate boot partitions add further prerequisites.

Preserve the failed boot’s journal when available. A wrong /etc/fstab entry, missing root device, and service configuration error require different repairs. Verify the repaired system through a planned reboot before considering the boot incident closed.

Linux example — 23.15

Inspect previous boot evidence if retained.

What to check: Use the lab console when the machine cannot reach a usable shell.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.15 Boot Failures

39. 23.16 Using Logs as Evidence

Logs are observations produced by software under particular permissions, clocks, retention, and rate limits. A missing event can mean no event occurred, or that collection, visibility, or retention failed. State the coverage limitation.

Correlate request IDs, service identities, and timestamps across layers. Record time zones and clock offsets. Keep original records protected, and use sanitized copies for collaboration. Do not alter the original log to make a cleaner narrative.

Distinguish what a log says from what you infer. “The worker reported EACCES at 10:03” is an observation. “A deployment changed directory permissions” is a hypothesis until change evidence supports it.

Linux example — 23.16

Use a bounded time window with stable timestamps.

What to check: Align service, client, and kernel events; missing logs are a coverage limitation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.16 Using Logs as Evidence

40. 23.16 Using Logs as Evidence · example 1

Logs are observations produced by software under particular permissions, clocks, retention, and rate limits. A missing event can mean no event occurred, or that collection, visibility, or retention failed. State the coverage limitation.

Correlate request IDs, service identities, and timestamps across layers. Record time zones and clock offsets. Keep original records protected, and use sanitized copies for collaboration. Do not alter the original log to make a cleaner narrative.

Distinguish what a log says from what you infer. “The worker reported EACCES at 10:03” is an observation. “A deployment changed directory permissions” is a hypothesis until change evidence supports it.

Linux example — 23.16

Use a bounded time window with stable timestamps.

What to check: Align service, client, and kernel events; missing logs are a coverage limitation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.16 Using Logs as Evidence

41. 23.17 Root-Cause Analysis

Root-cause analysis explains the causal chain and identifies changes that reduce recurrence or impact. It should include the trigger, underlying conditions, detection gaps, recovery friction, and controls that did or did not work.

“Human error” is usually too broad to guide improvement. Ask why the system allowed a risky action, why validation missed it, and why rollback was difficult. That does not remove accountability; it turns accountability into specific engineering actions.

Assign each corrective action an owner, due date, and verification method. Avoid claiming certainty when evidence is incomplete. A well-supported likely cause with a discriminating follow-up test is more useful than a confident story invented after service recovery.

Linux example — 23.17

Write a root-cause record with evidence and tests.

What to check: Distinguish an observed cause from a plausible hypothesis and from the command used to repair it.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — 23.17 Root-Cause Analysis

43. Observation and competing hypotheses

After a deployment, systemctl is-active nginx succeeds, but the client receives the distribution welcome page rather than the HarborStatus marker. The naive response is to restart NGINX. That may do nothing because the process is already serving exactly the configuration selected by the request.

Consider three hypotheses: the client reached another server; the intended configuration was not loaded; or the request selected the default virtual host. Each predicts a different comparison.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Observation and competing hypotheses

44. Discriminating tests

Run the loopback request on web1. Then run a client request using --resolve with the verified address. Inspect the loaded include path and a bounded access-log window. Do not publish nginx -T output without reviewing it for sensitive values.

Suppose the correctly named loopback and --resolve requests both return the HarborStatus marker, while a plain IP request returns the welcome page. That observation supports virtual-host selection, not a broken daemon. If ordinary named requests still fail, investigate DNS or an intermediary next.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Discriminating tests

45. Discriminating tests · example 1

Run the loopback request on web1. Then run a client request using --resolve with the verified address. Inspect the loaded include path and a bounded access-log window. Do not publish nginx -T output without reviewing it for sensitive values.

Suppose the correctly named loopback and --resolve requests both return the HarborStatus marker, while a plain IP request returns the welcome page. That observation supports virtual-host selection, not a broken daemon. If ordinary named requests still fail, investigate DNS or an intermediary next.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Discriminating tests

46. Repair and verification

Correct the client’s requested name or the intended default-site policy according to requirements. Do not make HarborStatus the default solely to hide a wrong URL unless that behavior is desired. Retest named requests, unknown-host behavior, and logs from the real client.

The root-cause record should state the actual contract mismatch and the missing deployment test. Add a named-host acceptance check so future releases do not rely on process status alone.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Repair and verification

47. Practice and implementation lab

Take one symptom and write three plausible causes before touching the VM. For each, choose a test whose outcomes separate it from the others. Have another learner inject one bounded configuration fault and require an evidence record before a repair.

Check your understanding. Does temporal correlation prove causality? No. Is service restoration the same as completed analysis? No. Should missing evidence be labeled unknown rather than invented? Yes.

Chapter takeaway. A reliable investigation preserves facts, narrows hypotheses, restores service safely, and converts evidence into verified prevention.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch025.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

48. Pick evidence that distinguishes competing causes

Select the failed layer from fixtures before changing packages or routes. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Pick evidence that distinguishes competing causes
